A1.justification: Both complete 92-page PDFs describe the same research work, with matching main sections and Appendices A-E. Text extraction and visual inspection support reliable comparison of their equations, tables, figures and appendix material.

before.justification: v4 reports original LLM decision-making and regret-loss training experiments in Sections 3 and 5.4, with further empirical results in Appendices C and E.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experiments, including online learning, repeated games, recommendation and negotiation case studies, and trained-Transformer analyses.

M1.justification: Section 2.2 corrects the stated Transformer clipping computation from reversed bounds to clipping within [-R,R]. This is a local model-specification correction; regret-loss and the remaining architecture and procedures are retained, without evidence of an implementation change.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same synthetic loss environments, full-information and bandit tasks, repeated games, adversarial scenarios, and recommendation and negotiation case studies, including Appendix C.10.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged within corresponding experiments, including FTRL/FTPL and their variants, the compared LLMs, and Table 2's Thompson Sampling, UCB and prompt configurations.

E3.justification: Experimental horizons, loss generation, feedback procedures, metrics, model sizes and training budgets are retained. The fitting split in Appendix D.9 and training settings in E.11-E.12 also remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Both retain history-summary comparisons, prompt ablations, application case studies, parameter-convergence analyses and regret-loss N/k ablations (Appendices C.6-C.10 and E.8-E.12). No analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Error-bar interpretation, statistical tests and repeated-run counts remain unchanged. Appendix E.8.1 merely rephrases the existing statement that experiments were repeated 10 times; it does not report additional runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1-3 and corresponding main-text and appendix plots retain their numerical entries, curves and findings. For example, Table 3 reports GPT-4's full-information gradual-variation dynamic regret as 12.61 ± 7.01 in both versions.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 changes min(-R,max(R,Z)) to min(R,max(-R,Z)), correcting a definition that previously returned constant -R for positive R. Theorems and proofs are retained; Equation (B.1)'s FTPL time-index shift is equivalent reindexing.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about observed no-regret behavior and failures, the conditional connection to FTPL, and regret-loss with statistical and optimization guarantees.

C2.justification: Interpretations involving trend prediction, randomization and summarized history are retained. Section 6 preserves the limitations concerning hypothetical pre-training assumptions, modest model scale, regret notions and numerical-payoff settings.

D1.justification: Prompts, loss reweighting, fitting instructions and training details remain unchanged. Appendix E.11 still specifies four layers, one head, Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 512, and 2,000 or 9,000 epochs.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive research positioning are retained, including the concurrent-work comparison in Appendix A. Bibliographic edits correct venue and title typos without adding or removing cited research.

P1.justification: v5 makes localized wording and grammar edits, standardizes appendix cross-references, removes the Introduction's unresolved literature-review reference to '??', and shortens acknowledgements and funding text. The section organization is retained.

P2.justification: There are small caption corrections, including Figures 3.4, 3.5 and C.3-C.4, and local layout reflow. References begin on page 20 instead of 21. Figures and tables retain their displays and organization.

improvement.justification: v5 corrects the invalid clipping formula, removes a broken Introduction reference, and improves prose, captions and bibliographic accuracy. These provide a limited gain in mathematical precision and readability; the empirical evidence, substantive theory and main conclusions remain stable.
